content: TNX-901 is an experimental drug undergoing testing at the National Jewish Medical and Research Center and other facilities across the United States. The drug is believed to have the potential to prevent allergic reactions to trace amounts of peanuts, such as those that might remain in processed foods. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted TNX-901 fast-track status, a designation given to drugs that address unmet medical needs for which no current treatments exist. The drug is developed by Tanox, a biotechnology company based in Houston. However, its development has been entangled in legal disputes. The controversy stems from claims that the drug is based on anti-asthma research funded by Genentech and Novartis. These legal battles have delayed the progress of clinical trials for TNX-901. TNX-901 functions as an anti-IgE antibody. Immunoglobulin E (IgE) is a type of antibody that plays a central role in allergic reactions and severe asthma attacks. By binding to IgE, TNX-901 prevents it from triggering the cascade of events that lead to an allergic reaction. In clinical trials, individuals with severe peanut allergies who previously experienced symptoms after consuming the equivalent of half a peanut were able to tolerate up to nine peanuts before showing any allergic symptoms. It is important to note, however, that the study did not include individuals with life-threatening peanut allergies caused by trace amounts of peanuts. A similar drug, Xolair (generic name: Omalizumab), is already available on the market for the treatment of asthma. However, Xolair is not currently approved for use in treating food allergies, including peanut allergies. The development and release of TNX-901 have been further complicated by a lawsuit from Xolair's manufacturer, which accused Tanox of patent infringement. Although it is technically possible for a physician to prescribe Xolair off-label for food allergies, most health insurance providers will not cover the cost without FDA approval for this specific use. As a result, patients would face out-of-pocket expenses of approximately $1,000 per month. In recent developments, Tanox has decided to halt further work on TNX-901 in exchange for financial compensation from Genentech and Novartis. The three companies have agreed to collaborate on researching the potential use of Xolair for peanut allergies instead of continuing with TNX-901. As of July 2004, Xolair entered Phase II clinical trials to evaluate its efficacy in treating peanut allergies.
